answer.answer: PVE34 was the best fixed Nyx profile for the older 10M data band, establishing clean throughput and ordinary restart recovery—not a permanent worker-count rule. Later autonomy evidence superseded that operating model: current code exceeded 1k PGCR/sec while adapting fetch, batch, and DB lanes by scenario. The next safe experiment is a bounded longer alpha soak with learned priors and full integrity/host-pressure gates, after the dirty autonomy work is packaged into reviewable commits.

claims.value: Historical 10M checkpoint: `split-lanes-64f-pve34-pvp2-other1-200k-to10m-20260523T115711Z` inserted `210624` rows, finished at `10.019M`, and crossed `10,000,000` at elapsed `442s`. Its steady average over elapsed `220-490s` was about `403/sec`, late pre-stop average about `408/sec`, and drain average about `372/sec`, with `0` parser errors, retries, duplicates, or terminal markers. Validation passed summary recompute for `1-10019225`, sampled membership recompute, final-chunk S3 and coverage windows, and unchanged protected D2 Redis counts. This established PVE34—with `64` fetch, PVE/PVP/other DB workers `34/2/1`, and membership sharding off—as the best practical fixed Nyx profile for that data band; it also showed that DB/write coordination, rather than fetch, limited throughput despite idle headroom. It did not establish PVE34 as a universal configuration.

The durable 2026-05-25 evidence superseded fixed-profile tuning as the operating model. Fully autonomous parsing became the goal, worker counts became evidence rather than identity, and source-level `112` semantics were removed. The autoscaler gained active/shadow decisions, cooldowns, rollback, bad-trial memory, path-independent fetch recovery, hot-lane pressure detection, dynamic worker retirement, and batch tuning with `128` as a learned keeper-family ceiling rather than a law. Scenario results showed why one fixed profile is invalid: alpha reached avg `1083.1 PGCR/sec`, steady `1122.9/sec`, final/max `1201.8/sec`; a corrected alpha reduced fetch to `32`, rolled back, and raised it again on real underfeed; gamma S3 reached avg `2141.3/sec`, steady `2243.0/sec`, final/max `2469.0/sec`; sustained `760ms` beta latency correctly scaled fetch to `128` while holding about `125-131/sec`; and delta scarcity reduced fetch/retry to floor `4`. DB rebalancing therefore remains scenario-specific and reversible—alpha often rejects `35/6 -> 36/5`, while gamma abundance may accept it. Learned priors are preferred for production-style long runs, with slow starts reserved for recovery proofs.

claims.value: Non-negotiable integrity/recovery model: data integrity beats throughput; autoscaler state is optimization state, never correctness state; DB rows are truth; raw marker commits travel with summaries; and normal parser restart from DB truth is the only recovery mechanism. Stop/drain may discard uncommitted in-memory fetch/retry jobs and drain DB queues that already own fetched PGCRs; the next normal run must recover the tail. Cortex must never enter the parser DB-write path, parser-owned S3 reads remain in the parser fetch path, and D2 protected Redis namespaces remain read-only. Rejected correctness crutches stay rejected: no `summary_time`, no `raw_pgcrs_players`, no D1 rebuild/recompute path, no parser-state correctness table, and no Cortex S3 replay into DB writes. Failed startup rows retry immediately; consecutive cache-stat/DB-availability failures stop the parser instead of masquerading as cache pressure; cache high-water must still allow the normal raw commit needed to complete the earliest rollup window; verified S3 batches use idempotent skip/recovery with preserved 1000-PGCR economics. Every serious run must retain contiguous raw coverage by count, `raw_failed_pgcrs=0`, S3 ledger/readback verification, only a normal partial cache tail, protected D2 Redis counts, Datadog visibility, Redis health, MySQL/host pressure evidence, and confirmation that no parser/Cortex process remains after a bounded run. Hard-kill/restart recovery must be proved before any unattended long run. The historical PVE34 recovery supports this contract: a normal restart found `1,336` gap ranges / `1,376` missing IDs, queued them automatically, and restored count-contiguous state through `9,808,601` without manual gap repair.

claims.value: Next safe work is not another fixed PVE34 comparison or durable-learning expansion. First package the large dirty autonomy worktree into small reviewable commits. Then run a bounded longer alpha historical-backparse soak using learned priors, keeping host/MySQL memory, CPU, and pressure inside the decision loop. Preserve reversible fixed-budget DB trials—move one worker at a time and accept or roll back—and treat batch `128` only as the current keeper ceiling. Score the experiment with `dev/scripts/d1-milestone-status.sh`, contiguous raw coverage, `raw_failed_pgcrs=0`, S3 ledger/readback, a normal partial cache tail, unchanged protected D2 Redis counts, Datadog visibility, Redis health, host/MySQL pressure, and no remaining parser/Cortex process. Do not promote it to an unattended long run until the current autonomy code has its own hard-kill/normal-restart proof. Durable controller persistence remains deferred until in-process behavior is calm and simple.

checkpoint.objective: Resume D1 parser performance/autonomy work by reconciling the older fixed-profile 10M Nyx result with the later durable autonomous-controller model without weakening correctness.
current_state: Historical and superseded: PVE34 (`64` fetch, `34/2/1` DB lanes, membership sharding off) crossed 10M cleanly at about `403/sec` steady and proved ordinary recovery after a hard kill.
Current durable evidence: scenario-aware autonomy has clean alpha throughput above 1k PGCR/sec and distinct beta, gamma, and delta behavior; fixed worker counts are no longer policy.

Verified integrity contract: DB truth, transactional raw-marker/summary commits, normal restart recovery, parser-owned S3 reads, no Cortex DB replay, protected D2 Redis read-only, and full validation gates.

Incomplete work: the autonomy worktree was recorded as large and dirty; longer alpha, beta recovery, delta cadence, gamma DB-lane tuning, rollup-worker autonomy, and durable controller persistence remained open.
decisions: Treat PVE34 as a historical fixed-profile baseline, not a default or identity.
Prefer learned priors and scenario-specific reversible control decisions.
Keep batch `128` as a keeper ceiling, not a universal law.
Do not add correctness scaffolding, replay/rebuild modes, or persistent controller state before in-process behavior is calm.
Run the next alpha soak bounded; require a current-code hard-kill/restart proof before unattended operation.
open_questions: How does host/MySQL pressure evolve during a longer current-code alpha soak?
Does beta fetch capacity reliably scale back down after artificial latency is removed?
What production cadence and fetch/batch policy best fit delta slow-edge behavior?
Which fixed-budget DB-lane balance is best under gamma S3 abundance?
Should rollup worker count remain configurable or become actively autotuned?
next_actions: Package the dirty autonomy work into small reviewable commits.
Run focused tests and review the exact candidate before experimentation.
Execute a bounded longer alpha soak with learned priors and complete host/MySQL telemetry.
Apply every integrity gate and confirm parser/Cortex termination after the run.
Perform a current-code hard-kill followed by ordinary restart recovery before considering an unattended long run.
Defer durable controller learning/persistence until the simpler in-process controller is stable.

answer.answer: Revised checkpoint: abandon the single dense mega-base for now. Under the level-0 Base Core’s 1,000-capacity ceiling, build a modular backbone-and-spurs factory with remote extraction, buffered single-item lines, dedicated export launchers, and one separately supplied defense circuit. Use only confirmed Update 1 rails and treat advanced or hidden database entries as unavailable until verified in-game.

claims.value: Current fact: the save is constrained to a level-0 Base Core with 1,000 capacity, and exceeding that capacity disables Fire Wave protection. Revised proposal: replace the earlier dense mega-base with a modular backbone-and-spurs architecture—small production districts near the protected core plus distributed mining outposts connected by rail trunks—and reserve capacity rather than planning to consume the full 1,000. Keep high-heat machinery out of the present design: a Constructorizer uses 500 heat and a Facturer uses 650, so those two alone exceed the entire level-0 budget. Use only Update 1 content; Rail v.4, Rail v.5, hidden buildings, and future-facing level 10–15/endgame content are excluded.

Live logistics proposal: use confirmed Update 1 Rail v.1/v.2/v.3 only, with capacities of 120/240/480 items/min. Rails also conduct electricity, so use item-specific mining spurs feeding an aggregated power-and-freight backbone; upgrade only where measured flow requires it. Match source rates directly: Ore Excavator v.1 produces 60/120/240 items/min on Impure/Normal/Pure nodes, while Helium-3 and Sulfur Extractors each produce 240/min; therefore a Normal v.1 ore node fits one Rail v.1, a Pure v.1 node or one Helium-3/Sulfur extractor fits one Rail v.2, and aggregation up to 480/min fits Rail v.3. Buffer each important single-item line with Storage Depot v.1 (400) or v.2 (1,600). Do not depend on Multistorage (Clever L12), Cargo Dispatcher/Receiver (Clever L7), Roundabout Rail Connector (Clever L8), or other later unlocks for the initial level-0 layout.

Exports proposal: give each actively exported product its own Orbital Cargo Launcher, because each launcher has exactly one input, and feed it from a dedicated 400- or 1,600-item single-product depot so production interruptions do not immediately starve reputation flow; add export products one at a time within the level-0 heat budget. Defense provision: establish one ammo-production reserve and defense spur. If only Defense Turret t1 is available, replenish it manually; if Defense Tower t2 is unlocked in the live Update 1 save, supply it over a thin Rail v.1 ammo loop. Keep Fire Wave protection intact by remaining below the Base Core’s 1,000-capacity limit.

Open in-game verification questions: (1) record the save’s actually unlocked rail, storage, exporter, machine, generator, and turret tiers before construction; (2) measure current Base Core load and verify the real capacity contribution of Base Core Amplifier v.1/v.2—the site descriptions say +50/+20 capacity, while data temperature fields say −250/−20; (3) test whether Rail Modulator merges are round-robin or priority-based; (4) test whether Multirail lanes have independent throughput or share a limit; (5) measure Drone Station coverage radius; (6) verify whether Delivery Storage is obtainable in Update 1, since it is site-flagged hidden; and (7) validate actual line throughput and buffer drain under sustained production and export before expanding a district.

checkpoint.objective: Replace the obsolete mega-base concept with an Update 1-only factory plan that remains safe under the save’s level-0 Base Core constraint while supporting production, logistics, buffered exports, and defense.
current_state: Current save constraint supplied by the task: Base Core level 0.
Authoritative corpus capacity table gives level 0 a 1,000-capacity budget; exceeding it disables Fire Wave protection.
Confirmed Update 1 transport tiers are Rail v.1/v.2/v.3 at 120/240/480 items/min; Rail v.4/v.5 and hidden/future-facing content are excluded.
The checkpoint is an evidence-backed proposal, not a verified in-game build or measured runtime result.
decisions: Supersede the earlier dense mega-base idea with modular production districts and distributed extraction connected by backbone-and-spur rails.
Retain deliberate unused Base Core capacity; do not design up to or beyond 1,000.
Use one item per line where practical and place 400- or 1,600-item buffers before critical consumers and each active exporter.
Use dedicated one-input Orbital Cargo Launchers rather than mixing export products.
Provision one ammo reserve and defense spur, with manual t1 replenishment or rail-fed t2 replenishment according to the save’s actual unlock state.
Exclude unverified hidden entries and all known post-Update 1 rail tiers/content.
open_questions: Which Update 1 buildings and tiers are actually unlocked in this save?
What is the current measured Base Core load and safe reserve margin?
What capacity do Amplifier v.1 and v.2 really add in the live build?
How do Rail Modulator merge arbitration, Multirail throughput, and Drone Station coverage behave?
Is Delivery Storage obtainable in Update 1?
Do sustained measured flows match the planned rail capacities, buffer sizing, and export drain?
next_actions: Open the build menus and inventory; record every available rail, storage, exporter, production, power, and defense building.
Read the Base Core UI and inventory the existing powered buildings to establish current load before placing anything.
Run a small Rail v.1 source-to-buffer-to-consumer test, then repeat with an exporter to measure steady-state throughput and drain.
Test one merge under competing inputs, each Multirail lane under simultaneous load if unlocked, and Drone Station reach at increasing distances.
Place or inspect each available amplifier and record the before/after Base Core capacity.
Build the first bounded district only after those measurements; keep a written heat ledger and stop expansion before protection is threatened.
